final_answer:
Let

\[
R(x)=1-\frac{14}{3}x^2+\frac{21}{5}x^4.
\]

Then \(R(0)=1\), and \(R(x)^2\ge \mathbf 1_{\{0\}}(x)\) for every \(x\in[-1,1]\). Hence for any admissible \(X\),

\[
\mathbb P(X=0)\le \mathbb E[R(X)^2].
\]

Since \(R^2\) has degree \(8\), the moment assumptions imply

\[
\mathbb E[R(X)^2]=\frac12\int_{-1}^1 R(t)^2\,dt.
\]

Expanding,

\[
R(t)^2
=
1-\frac{28}{3}t^2+\frac{1358}{45}t^4-\frac{196}{5}t^6+\frac{441}{25}t^8.
\]

Using \(\frac12\int_{-1}^1 t^{2j}\,dt=\frac1{2j+1}\),

\[
\frac12\int_{-1}^1 R(t)^2\,dt
=
1-\frac{28}{9}+\frac{1358}{225}-\frac{196}{35}+\frac{441}{225}
=
\frac{64}{225}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\mathbb P(X=0)\le \frac{64}{225}.
\]

Now we show equality is attainable and classify it. The zeros of \(R\) away from \(0\) satisfy, with \(y=x^2\),

\[
1-\frac{14}{3}y+\frac{21}{5}y^2=0,
\]

so

\[
y=\frac{35\pm 2\sqrt{70}}{63}.
\]

Define

\[
a=\frac{35-2\sqrt{70}}{63},
\qquad
b=\frac{35+2\sqrt{70}}{63}.
\]

Equality in the bound requires \(X\) to be supported only on

\[
\{0,\pm\sqrt a,\pm\sqrt b\},
\]

because \(R(x)^2-\mathbf 1_{\{0\}}(x)\) must vanish almost surely.

Let

\[
\mathbb P(X=0)=\frac{64}{225},
\]

and put total masses \(U\) on the two points \(\pm\sqrt a\), and \(V\) on the two points \(\pm\sqrt b\). The even moment conditions force

\[
U+V=\frac{161}{225},\qquad Ua+Vb=\frac13.
\]

Solving gives

\[
U=\frac{161\sqrt{70}+455}{450\sqrt{70}},
\qquad
V=\frac{161\sqrt{70}-455}{450\sqrt{70}}.
\]

The odd moment conditions force symmetry between the positive and negative points, so the unique extremizing distribution is

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P(X=0)=\frac{64}{225}
}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P(X=\pm\sqrt a)
=
\frac{161\sqrt{70}+455}{900\sqrt{70}},
\qquad
\mathbb P(X=\pm\sqrt b)
=
\frac{161\sqrt{70}-455}{900\sqrt{70}},
}
\]

where

\[
\boxed{
a=\frac{35-2\sqrt{70}}{63},
\qquad
b=\frac{35+2\sqrt{70}}{63}.
}
\]

This distribution has all odd moments \(0\) by symmetry. Its even moments through degree \(8\) are \(1/3,1/5,1/7,1/9\), so it is admissible. Thus the maximum is exactly

\[
\boxed{\frac{64}{225}},
\]

attained uniquely by the distribution above.
